assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 model of credit cycles shows how collateral constraints turn small shocks into persistent, amplified fluctuations. It became the template for the financial-friction literature, and the 2007-09 crisis renewed its relevance. The conceptual contribution is deep and general.
assessment.attribution: The core model is clearly a two-author contribution. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the related financial accelerator and its empirical work, but the founding idea is Kiyotaki-Moore. Limiting the award to two names keeps the credit clean.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of citation, extension and use in policy models. The mechanism has stood up well in later empirical work on collateral and credit supply, and the prize has not yet recognised this strand beyond Bernanke's related work.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier Bernanke-Gertler financial accelerator could raise a question about how credit is divided.
Direct empirical identification of the collateral channel relies on later work by others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP demand-estimation framework, with later dynamic industry models, is a methodological advance that changed empirical industrial organisation. It supports merger review, antitrust and welfare analysis. Contributions are concrete, replicable and widely reused.
assessment.attribution: The 1995 BLP paper identifies Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes directly. Pakes also has separate work on dynamic games (Ericson-Pakes) and on estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made related contributions, so the longlist is broader than the proposed trio.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of use, with many applications showing the method is robust in practice. It is mature.
uncertainties: Some committee members may prefer to recognise earlier empirical-IO pioneers such as Bresnahan.
Identification and numerical-implementation concerns about BLP have been raised in later work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz's 2003 heterogeneous-firm model and Helpman's broader work on trade with increasing returns shifted the field from industry-level to firm-level analysis. They shaped how researchers measure selection, reallocation and gains from trade, and the predictions have been tested extensively against firm-level data.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the centrepiece. Helpman has a long, distinct body of work and co-authored the firm-heterogeneity papers (Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple). Redding has important later contributions, but two names capture the core.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of empirical validation. The 2008 prize to Krugman covered earlier trade theory without covering this firm-level wave.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a new discovery or an extension of the Krugman framework.
Quantitative gains-from-trade results are sensitive to model structure.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fairness and reciprocity models, together with the experimental evidence on strong reciprocity and costly punishment, established that social preferences are empirically robust and can be formalised. They changed contract, public-goods and labour-market theory. The core ultimatum and public-goods results replicate well across populations, which counts in favour of the evidence base.
assessment.attribution: Fehr-Schmidt (1999) provides the theory, and Fehr's experimental programme provides much of the evidence. Falk has made major empirical and cross-cultural contributions. Bolton-Ockenfels and Rabin made parallel contributions that are not credited here, so attribution is contested.
assessment.maturity: Twenty-five years of work. Behavioural economics has already been honoured (Kahneman, Smith, Thaler), but social preferences have not.
uncertainties: Parallel contributions by Bolton-Ockenfels and Rabin complicate attribution.
External validity of lab-based social-preference measures remains debated.
A specific heterogeneity or generalisation concern: inequity aversion fits some games better than others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian synthesis underlie modern central-bank analysis. The key elements are staggered pricing and contracts, the Taylor rule and the microfounded framework of Woodford. Policy impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: This is the most diffuse candidate, with eight names and several overlapping contributions (Calvo pricing, Taylor contracts, Woodford's framework, Galí-Gertler, Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans). Any three-person selection leaves out comparable contributors.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use, but also substantial criticism after the financial crisis, which led to the heterogeneous-agent extensions.
uncertainties: Attribution is hard to resolve and any trio is contestable.
Empirical performance of the canonical framework has been questioned, especially around the crisis and the 2021-23 inflation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) showed how misallocation of inputs across firms can account for a large share of cross-country income gaps. It reframed development and growth accounting in terms of micro-level distortions and generated an extensive empirical agenda.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the clear authors of the central paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is a closely parallel contribution. Restuccia is credited on the list, so the choice of two versus three names is a real question.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen years of influence. Measurement-sensitivity critiques are still being worked through.
uncertainties: Measured misallocation is sensitive to data quality and to markup and measurement error.
Parallel contribution from Restuccia-Rogerson affects who should be credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock research and the task-based approach to technology showed large and persistent local labour-market effects of trade and automation. The work is policy-relevant, especially for discussions of AI and displacement, and is empirically transparent.
assessment.attribution: Autor-Dorn-Hanson form a coherent trio on the trade-shock papers. The task framework also draws on Acemoglu-Autor and Autor-Levy-Murnane, and Katz is credited here as well, so the intellectual credit is shared across several groups.
assessment.maturity: A decade of replication, extension and debate. Some of the debate concerns specification choices, so conclusions on magnitudes are not final.
uncertainties: Shift-share identification has been scrutinised, and the results could be sensitive to exposure-design choices.
Overlap with the Acemoglu-Restrepo task literature complicates credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Chetty and collaborators used administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation, and developed methods that link research to policy evaluation (for example, Moving to Opportunity). The work is high-impact, transparent and based on large samples, which supports reliability.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure and the contributions are shared with a large collaborative team, so assigning credit to three people is difficult. Katz is credited through the Moving to Opportunity work.
assessment.maturity: The work is recent, mostly from the last decade. Some findings are still being replicated and extended in other countries, so confirmation is partial.
uncertainties: The work may be too recent to be a settled discovery.
Causal interpretation of place effects and sensitivity to data and methods remain under discussion.
Credit is spread across a large research team.
